lessons.title: Linguistic diversity and dialects
lessons.anelcac: Notions of linguistic diversity, dialects, names of languages, geographical classification
objectives: Becoming aware of the linguistic diversity of Cameroon (about 280 languages according to the LACAGEO Mini-Atlas)
Distinguish language, dialect and variant according to academic definitions
Naming Bulu and locating it in the geographical classification of the languages of Cameroon
Adopt an attitude of respect towards all languages

teacher.intro: Lesson: Linguistic diversity and dialects. Module: Module I — Cameroonian linguistic diversity.
steps: **Setting the context:** Display the map of the Linguistic Mini-Atlas of Cameroon. Ask students which languages are spoken in their family.
**Exploration:** Have students read the definitions in the Mini-Atlas (language, dialect, patois, national language). Locate Bulu in its linguistic region.
**Conceptualisation:** Explain the language / dialect distinction with examples: the Bulu, Ewondo, Eton and Mangisa dialects all belong to the Beti-Fang language (Mini-Atlas).
**Application:** Complete a table: name of the language, family, main region, ISO code.
**Assessment:** Each student gives an oral presentation of Bulu, indicating family and region.
teacher.freedom: The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas (2013) distinguishes about 280 living languages in Cameroon. The exact number varies according to the criteria (SIL: 274, Ethnologue: 279). Value all the languages cited.
teacher.tips: The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas (2013) distinguishes about 280 living languages in Cameroon. The exact number varies according to the criteria (SIL: 274, Ethnologue: 279). Value all the languages cited.

student.intro: Cameroon is one of the richest nations in the world in languages — the linguistic Mini-Atlas lists about 280! In this lesson, you discover the place of Bulu in this great family.
activities: Look at the Mini-Atlas map and find the area where Bulu is mainly spoken.
Copy and complete: Bulu belongs to the ___ family. It is mostly spoken in the ___ region.
According to the Mini-Atlas, how many living languages are there in the Bulu region? Note down this number.
Survey: ask an adult the name of the language in which they were raised and where it is spoken.
Memorise: **dialect** = an intelligible variant of the same language; **national language** = language of an ethnic group that does not extend beyond the borders of one State (ACA LAN).
student.memo: Cameroon has about **280 languages** according to the LACAGEO Mini-Atlas. Bulu belongs to a Cameroonian language family and has its own dialectal variants. According to the ACA LAN, a national language is the language of an ethnic group that does not extend beyond the borders of one State.

lessons.title: Classification of languages and linguistic atlas
lessons.anelcac: Classification of the languages of Cameroon: linguistic areas, families, ALCAM atlas
objectives: Name the main linguistic areas of Cameroon
Read and interpret an extract from a linguistic atlas (ALCAM / Mini-Atlas)
Classify Bulu according to its typological criteria
Producing a short text presenting Bulu

teacher.intro: Lesson: Classification of languages and linguistic atlas. Module: Module I — Cameroonian linguistic diversity.
steps: **Setting the context:** Go back over the definitions. How many language families do students remember?
**Presentation:** The 8 world language families according to Ethnologue (Niger-Kordofanian, Nilo-Saharan, Afro-Asiatic…). Place Cameroonian languages within this whole.
**Explanation:** Show how to find Bulu in the ALCAM: ISO code, family, location.
**Guided practice:** In pairs, students find 3 languages neighbouring Bulu and note their ISO codes.
**Production:** 5-line paragraph presenting Bulu (family, region, speakers, distinctive feature).
teacher.freedom: The online ALCAM is on the Mozilla Data Collective. The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas covers all the administrative regions with maps and statistics.
teacher.tips: The online ALCAM is on the Mozilla Data Collective. The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas covers all the administrative regions with maps and statistics.

student.intro: A linguistic atlas is a specialised map. The ALCAM (Atlas of the Languages of Cameroon) and the LACAGEO Mini-Atlas let you locate Bulu precisely.
activities: On the Mini-Atlas map, locate Bulu and note its administrative region.
List 3 languages whose area is adjacent to that of Bulu.
Classify these 4 languages in a table: Language | Family | Main region.
Write an introductory paragraph about Bulu with at least 5 pieces of information taken from the atlas.
Memorise: **ISO 639** = international language codes; **ALCAM** = Atlas des Langues du Cameroun.
student.memo: The **ALCAM** and the **LACAGEO Mini-Atlas** list and locate all the national languages of Cameroon. Cameroon has 8 main language families. Bulu appears there with its family and its location. Knowing how to read a linguistic atlas is reading the history of peoples.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants
lessons.title: Vowels of Bulu
lessons.anelcac: AGLC vowels — simple, specific, complex
objectives: Identify the simple vowels of the phonological system of Bulu
Recognising specific vowels absent from French
Pronouncing vowels correctly in the context of a word
Transcribing words containing vowels according to AGLC

vocabulary.frenchText: the man fell from the tree

teacher.intro: Lesson: Bulu vowels. Module: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write known words in Bulu on the board and ask which sounds students hear.
**Presentation:** Introduce the AGLC. Write the simple vowels of Bulu on the board, articulating them clearly.
**Explanation:** Vowels specific to Bulu that are absent from French (nasal, particular openness…). Listening and repetition exercises.
**Application:** List of 10 words — students underline the vowels and indicate: simple or specific.
**Assessment:** Dictation of 5 simple words — students transcribe them with the correct vowels.
teacher.freedom: Use the examples from the platform's ALCAM vocabulary. For each specific vowel, give a memorable key word.
teacher.tips: Use the examples from the platform's ALCAM vocabulary. For each specific vowel, give a memorable key word.

student.intro: Every language has its own sounds. In Bulu, some vowels do not exist in French. This lesson teaches you to hear, pronounce and write them.
activities: Listen to the recordings of the Bulu vocabulary and identify the vowels you hear.
Classify the vowels: **Shared with French** | **Specific to Bulu**.
Transcribe the 5 dictated words, taking care to note each vowel correctly.
Find 3 words in Bulu for each specific vowel and write them down.
Memorise: **AGLC** = Alphabet Général des Langues Camerounaises, the official reference.
student.memo: The vowel system of **Bulu** includes simple vowels and specific vowels (e.g. nasalised vowels). They are written using the **AGLC**. Mastery of vowels is the basis of reading and writing in Bulu.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants
lessons.title: Bulu consonants and written production
lessons.anelcac: Consonants — simple, specific, complex; written production of vowels and consonants
objectives: Identify the consonant system of Bulu
Recognising specific consonants absent from French
Articulate consonants correctly in context
Writing words with vowels and consonants correctly notated

vocabulary.frenchText: the man fell from the tree

teacher.intro: Lesson: Bulu consonants and written production. Module: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants.
steps: **Setting the context:** Recall the vowels. What is a consonant?
**Presentation:** Table of Bulu consonants according to the AGLC. Stress the specific consonants (labio-velars, prenasalised, implosives…).
**Explanation:** Articulating difficult consonants: in isolation → syllable → word.
**Application:** Minimal pairs: listening to words that differ only by one consonant.
**Production:** 5 simple sentences in Bulu with careful consonant transcription.
teacher.freedom: Implosive and prenasalised consonants are often the most difficult for students who learned to read and write in French. Repeat the listening activities many times.
teacher.tips: Implosive and prenasalised consonants are often the most difficult for students who learned to read and write in French. Repeat the listening activities many times.

student.intro: After the vowels, here are the consonants of Bulu! Some are unique — you will only hear them in Bulu and in a few neighbouring African languages.
activities: Listen to the minimal pairs and tick the word you hear (e.g. bìlí / pìlí).
Transcribe 5 dictated words, paying attention to the specific consonants.
Find in the vocabulary all the words containing a prenasalised consonant. How many do you find?
Compose 3 simple sentences in Bulu, each with at least one specific consonant.
Memorise: **minimal pair** = two words identical except for one phoneme.
student.memo: The consonant system of **Bulu** includes consonants shared with French and specific consonants (implosives, prenasalised, labio-velars…). Writing them according to the **AGLC** is essential for reading and writing.

lessons.title: Definition and functions of tones
lessons.anelcac: Tones — definition, function, presentation; simple tones (high, low, mid)
objectives: Define tone as a distinctive feature of tone languages
Distinguish lexical tone from grammatical tone
Identify the simple tones of Bulu
Transcribing words with their tones according to AGLC

vocabulary.frenchText: the ball of (cassava, maize, millet, banana) is round

teacher.intro: Lesson: Definition and function of tones. Module: Module III — Suprasegmental phonology: tones.
steps: **Setting the context:** Say two Bulu words that are written the same but have different tones and different meanings.
**Presentation:** Define tone. Present the simple tones of Bulu and their AGLC diacritics.
**Explanation:** Simple tones: high (´), low (`), mid (¯). Have students repeat each tone.
**Application:** Match recorded words with their tone notation.
**Assessment:** Dictation of 5 words — students note the tones.
teacher.freedom: Singing the tones helps to memorise them. Use a flute or whistle the tonal melodies.
teacher.tips: Singing the tones helps to memorise them. Use a flute or whistle the tonal melodies.

student.intro: Bulu is a tonal language: the pitch of your voice changes the meaning of the word! You will learn to hear and write down these tones.
activities: Listen to the pairs of words. For each pair, are the tones the same or different?
Transcribe 5 words with their tones using the AGLC diacritics (´ ` ¯).
Find 2 words in the vocabulary that differ only in tone. What does each one mean?
Sing the tones of a 3-syllable word as High-Low-High, then Low-High-Low. What difference do you hear?
Memorise: high tone = ´ ; low tone = ` ; mid tone = ¯.
student.memo: In **Bulu**, tone is phonological: it distinguishes words with different meanings. The **simple tones** are high (´), low (`), and sometimes mid (¯). They are written using the **AGLC** diacritics.

lessons.title: Complex tones and tone-marked written production
lessons.anelcac: Complex tones (rising, falling); finding the tone of a word; tonal written production
objectives: Identify the complex tones of Bulu (rising, falling)
Finding the tone of a word by the isolation method
Transcribing sentences with full tone marking
Producing a short text in Bulu with correct tones

vocabulary.frenchText: the ball of (cassava, maize, millet, banana) is round

teacher.intro: Lesson: Complex tones and tonal written production. Module: Module III — Suprasegmental phonology: tones.
steps: **Setting the context:** Recall the simple tones. Announce that some syllables carry two tones in succession.
**Presentation:** Complex tones: falling (̂), rising (̌). Let students hear them and reproduce them.
**Explanation:** Isolation method: say the word with an artificial high tone, then a low one, and listen to which sounds natural.
**Application:** Students find the tone of 10 words in Bulu using the isolation method.
**Production:** Dialogue of 6 lines in Bulu with complete tone notation.
teacher.freedom: The complex falling tone is often the most frequent. Start with it before the rising tone.
teacher.tips: The complex falling tone is often the most frequent. Start with it before the rising tone.

student.intro: You know the simple tones. Now for the complex tones of Bulu — syllables that rise and fall at the same time!
activities: Listen to the recorded words and sort them: Simple tone | Complex tone.
Apply the isolation method to 5 words: say them high, then low, and note the tone you perceive.
Transcribe a dialogue of 4 lines in Bulu with all the tones marked.
Write a 3-sentence text in Bulu about an action from your daily life, with tone marking.
Memorise: falling tone = ̂ ; rising tone = ̌.
student.memo: The **complex tones** of **Bulu** (falling ̂, rising ̌) are melodic movements on a single syllable. The **isolation method** makes it possible to find the tone of an unknown word. A transcription in Bulu without tones is incomplete.

lessons.title: The noun base and noun classes
lessons.anelcac: NP: constituents, base noun + affixes, noun classes, personal pronouns
objectives: Identify the structure of the noun in Bulu (base + affixes)
Recognising the noun classes of Bulu
Form the singular and plural of nouns
Use the personal pronouns corresponding to noun classes

vocabulary.frenchText: the man is hungry for meat

teacher.intro: Lesson: The noun base and noun classes. Module: Module IV — The noun phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write a noun in Bulu in the singular and plural. What changes?
**Presentation:** Noun class: in Bantu and Bantoid languages, nouns are grouped into classes marked by prefixes.
**Explanation:** Main noun classes of Bulu with singular and plural prefixes.
**Application:** Table: singular → plural for 10 nouns.
**Assessment:** Identify the noun class of 5 nouns.
teacher.freedom: Start from the nouns that students already use. Noun classes often correspond to semantic categories (humans, animals, objects…).
teacher.tips: Start from the nouns that students already use. Noun classes often correspond to semantic categories (humans, animals, objects…).

student.intro: In Bulu, nouns are organised into **classes**. Each class has its own prefixes for the singular and plural — a much richer system than gender in French!
activities: Using the Bulu vocabulary, make a table: Singular | Plural | Noun class.
Identify the class prefix in each noun. Highlight it.
Put the following 5 nouns into the plural by changing the prefix according to the class.
Match each noun with its corresponding class pronoun.
Memorise: **noun class** = grammatical category of nouns, marked by prefixes.
student.memo: In **Bulu**, nouns are organised into **noun classes** marked by prefixes. A change of prefix indicates number. Pronouns, adjectives and verbs agree with the class of the noun.

lessons.title: Noun determiners
lessons.anelcac: Determiners: possessives, demonstratives, numerals, indefinites, interrogatives; noun class agreement
objectives: Identify the different types of determiners in Bulu
Make determiners agree with the noun according to the noun class
Build complex noun phrases
Producing sentences with complete NPs

vocabulary.frenchText: the man is hungry for meat

teacher.intro: Lesson: Noun determiners. Module: Module IV — The noun phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write a simple noun phrase. How can it be enriched?
**Presentation:** Determiners in Bulu: possessives, demonstratives, numerals, indefinites, interrogatives.
**Explanation:** Each determiner agrees with the class of the noun (same class prefix or suffix).
**Application:** Complete noun phrases with the correct determiner according to the class.
**Production:** 5 complex noun phrases (noun + 2 determiners) used in sentences.
teacher.freedom: Stress class agreement — one of the most distinctive features of Bulu compared with French.
teacher.tips: Stress class agreement — one of the most distinctive features of Bulu compared with French.

student.intro: A noun with its determiners becomes much more precise! In Bulu, determiners agree with the **noun class**.
activities: Complete the NPs with the correct possessive determiner according to the noun class.
Underline the determiners in 5 sentences in Bulu and identify their type.
Turn each simple noun phrase into a complex noun phrase by adding a demonstrative and a numeral.
Write 5 sentences in Bulu with at least two determiners per noun phrase.
Memorise: **class agreement** = the determiner changes form according to the noun class.
student.memo: In **Bulu**, all determiners (possessives, demonstratives, numerals, indefinites, interrogatives) agree with the **noun class** of the noun. A **complex NP** = noun + nominal base + agreeing determiners.

lessons.title: The verb stem and conjugation
lessons.anelcac: VP: constituents, stem, affixes, conjugation, verb tenses
objectives: Identify the verb stem and the conjugation affixes in Bulu
Conjugate a verb in the main tenses
Analyse the morphological structure of a verb form
Use verb forms correctly in sentences

vocabulary.langText: mà kə́ lóm mɔ́n á-kə̀-dzə́ŋ mə̀ndíp
vocabulary.frenchText: I sent the child to fetch water
a) he was walking while singing .

vocabulary.langText: bóngó bə́mbə́-bə́-kə̀lə̀k mìmbíl, bə́ dzə́mə̀k; bə́ wàè
vocabulary.frenchText: the children ran, danced and laughed
the man fell from the tree

vocabulary.langText: àngá kə̀ éyōŋ wà kə́ kwí
ànɔ̀n ə̰́ndə̀tə̀ dáyə́lə̀ sə́sàlə̀ və̀ kɔ̀s
vocabulary.frenchText: it is birds that fly, not fish
the woman pours water into the calabash
they are not fighting, they are playing

teacher.intro: Lesson: The verb stem and conjugation. Module: Module V — The verb phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write a verb form in Bulu and ask students to identify the stem.
**Presentation:** Break down a verb form: subject prefix + TAM markers + stem + suffixes.
**Explanation:** Conjugation paradigm of a common verb in Bulu in several tenses.
**Application:** Conjugation table: 3 common verbs.
**Assessment:** Translate 5 sentences from French into Bulu.
teacher.freedom: The TAM system of Bulu is often richer than that of French. Start with the most commonly used tenses.
teacher.tips: The TAM system of Bulu is often richer than that of French. Start with the most commonly used tenses.

student.intro: The verb is the heart of the sentence in Bulu. It alone carries tense, aspect, mood and subject! In this lesson, you take apart the verbal mechanics.
activities: Break down 5 verb forms in Bulu: subject prefix | TAM marker | stem | suffix.
Conjugate the verb 'to eat' in Bulu in 3 different tenses for all persons.
Identify the tense of 5 sentences in Bulu and justify your answer.
Translate 3 sentences from French into Bulu, taking care with the conjugation.
Memorise: **TAM** = Tense-Aspect-Mood; this is what verbal affixes express in Bulu.
student.memo: In **Bulu**, a verb form = subject prefix + TAM markers + stem + suffixes. The **TAM** (Tense-Aspect-Mood) system expresses more precise temporal and aspectual nuances than in French.

lessons.title: Verbal moods and negation
lessons.anelcac: Moods: indicative, imperative; negation; written production of simple/complex VP
objectives: Identify and use the main verbal moods of Bulu
Form the verbal negation
Build simple and complex verb phrases
Producing a text with a variety of moods and aspects

vocabulary.langText: mà kə́ lóm mɔ́n á-kə̀-dzə́ŋ mə̀ndíp
vocabulary.frenchText: I sent the child to fetch water
a) he was walking while singing .

vocabulary.langText: bóngó bə́mbə́-bə́-kə̀lə̀k mìmbíl, bə́ dzə́mə̀k; bə́ wàè
vocabulary.frenchText: the children ran, danced and laughed
the man fell from the tree

vocabulary.langText: àngá kə̀ éyōŋ wà kə́ kwí
ànɔ̀n ə̰́ndə̀tə̀ dáyə́lə̀ sə́sàlə̀ və̀ kɔ̀s
vocabulary.frenchText: it is birds that fly, not fish
the woman pours water into the calabash
they are not fighting, they are playing

teacher.intro: Lesson: Verbal moods and negation. Module: Module V — The verb phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Give an order in Bulu. Which mood is used?
**Presentation:** Moods in Bulu: indicative, imperative, and other aspectual moods.
**Explanation:** Formation of the negative in Bulu: prefix, negative suffix, or particle.
**Application:** Turn 5 affirmative sentences into negative ones and vice versa.
**Production:** 8-sentence text alternating affirmation, negation and imperative.
teacher.freedom: Negation in Bulu can be double (framing the verb) or simple. Show both cases.
teacher.tips: Negation in Bulu can be double (framing the verb) or simple. Show both cases.

student.intro: Giving an order, expressing doubt, denying an action — each nuance has its own form in Bulu!
activities: Put the 5 given sentences into the negative form.
Turn these 5 statements into imperatives addressed to a friend.
Identify the mood and polarity (affirmative/negative) of each sentence in the text provided.
Write a dialogue of 6 lines including at least 2 imperatives and 2 negations.
Memorise: **mood** = the way of viewing the action; **negation** = grammatical marker denying the action.
student.memo: In **Bulu**, the main moods are the **indicative** and the **imperative**. **Negation** is marked by a particle or a specific affix. The diversity of moods is an expressive richness of Bulu.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module VI — The sentence in Bulu
lessons.title: The simple sentence and its types
lessons.anelcac: Simple, interrogative, negative and imperative sentence; word order
objectives: Analyse the structure of the simple sentence in Bulu
Distinguish the 4 types of sentences
Mastering the order of constituents
Producing varied simple sentences

vocabulary.frenchText: there is a big black stone over there.
there is a tall tree over there
I am taking a small stone.
he took a short stick (at that moment).
the calabash is full of water

teacher.intro: Lesson: The simple sentence and its types. Module: Module VI — The sentence in Bulu.
steps: **Setting the context:** Read a sentence in Bulu. Who does what?
**Presentation:** Basic constituent order in Bulu. Compare with French.
**Explanation:** The 4 sentence types from the same basic sentence.
**Application:** Turn declarative sentences into interrogative ones, then into negative ones.
**Production:** 8 varied sentences (2 per type) about school life.
teacher.freedom: Word order in Bulu may differ from French. This is a typological feature, not a mistake.
teacher.tips: Word order in Bulu may differ from French. This is a typological feature, not a mistake.

student.intro: A well-constructed sentence in Bulu follows precise rules. You learn the types of sentences and word order.
activities: Identify the order of constituents in 5 sentences in Bulu.
Turn 4 declarative sentences into yes/no questions.
Turn these 4 sentences into negatives.
Write 2 sentences of each type (declarative, interrogative, negative, imperative).
Memorise: the basic order in **Bulu** is typologically stable.
student.memo: The **simple sentence** in **Bulu** has a characteristic order of constituents. The 4 types (declarative, interrogative, negative, imperative) are formed with specific grammatical markers.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module VI — The sentence in Bulu
lessons.title: Logical connectors and the complex sentence
lessons.anelcac: Logical connectors, complex sentence, coordination, subordination; written production
objectives: Identify the logical connectors of Bulu
Distinguish coordination from subordination
Build complex sentences
Producing a coherent text with syntactic variety

vocabulary.frenchText: there is a big black stone over there.
there is a tall tree over there
I am taking a small stone.
he took a short stick (at that moment).
the calabash is full of water

teacher.intro: Lesson: Logical connectors and the complex sentence. Module: Module VI — The sentence in Bulu.
steps: **Setting the context:** Read a short story in Bulu. Which words link the sentences?
**Presentation:** Connectors in Bulu: coordinating and subordinating conjunctions.
**Explanation:** Complex sentence by coordination / by subordination. Examples in Bulu.
**Application:** Link 5 pairs of simple sentences with the appropriate connector.
**Production:** 10-sentence text on 'A day in my village' with 5 different connectors.
teacher.freedom: The connectors of Bulu often have French equivalents but with different syntactic positions.
teacher.tips: The connectors of Bulu often have French equivalents but with different syntactic positions.

student.intro: To tell stories and argue, you need to link your sentences. The **logical connectors** of Bulu are your tools!
activities: Underline all the connectors in the text provided.
Classify them: Addition | Cause | Consequence | Opposition | Time.
Link 5 pairs of sentences with the most appropriate connector.
Write a text of 8 sentences with at least 4 different connectors.
Memorise: coordination = same level; subordination = one sentence inside another.
student.memo: In **Bulu**, **logical connectors** make it possible to build coherent **complex sentences**. Varying syntactic structures improves the quality of written and spoken expression.

lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and interacting in Bulu
lessons.anelcac: Everyday communication situations: greetings, introductions, polite expressions
objectives: Mastering greeting formulas according to context
Introducing yourself and someone else in Bulu
Use polite and respectful expressions
Holding a short everyday conversation

teacher.intro: Lesson: Greeting, introducing yourself and interacting in Bulu. Module: Module VII — Everyday life (Level 1).
steps: **Setting the context:** Two students meet at the market. Act out the scene in French, then ask how to say it in Bulu.
**Presentation:** Greetings in Bulu according to the time of day, age and context.
**Explanation:** Formulas of respect towards elders, specific to Bulu culture.
**Role play:** In groups of 2, simulate encounters in various contexts (market, school, ceremony).
**Production:** Dialogue of 10 lines between two people of different generations.
teacher.freedom: Greeting rules reflect deep cultural values. Value the knowledge of students from families who speak the language.
teacher.tips: Greeting rules reflect deep cultural values. Value the knowledge of students from families who speak the language.

student.intro: Knowing how to greet in Bulu means respecting the culture! The greetings change depending on whom you greet and at what time.
activities: Complete the table of Bulu greetings: Time | Formula | Expected response.
Play role A: greeting an elder at the morning market.
Make up a dialogue of 8 lines between a child and their grandfather.
Note down 3 Bulu politeness formulas with no direct equivalent in French.
Memorise the morning and evening greeting formulas, and those for elders, in Bulu.
student.memo: **Greetings** in **Bulu** vary according to the time of day, status and social context. They reflect the community's values of respect and solidarity.

lessons.title: Express everyday needs and actions
lessons.anelcac: Real-life situations: shopping, requests for help, travelling, daily activities
objectives: Express everyday needs in Bulu
Describe daily activities
Use vocabulary for places and actions of everyday life
Producing a descriptive text on a typical day

teacher.intro: Lesson: Expressing everyday needs and actions. Module: Module VII — Everyday life (Level 1).
steps: **Setting the context:** Images of scenes from daily life — market, field, school, home. How can they be described in Bulu?
**Presentation:** Thematic vocabulary: food, travel, household activities.
**Simulation:** Market scene: buyer and seller in Bulu.
**Application:** Describe your day in Bulu (from waking up to going to bed).
**Production:** 10-sentence text: 'My day in Bulu'.
teacher.freedom: Everyday vocabulary is the most motivating. Link the ALCAM words to real situations.
teacher.tips: Everyday vocabulary is the most motivating. Link the ALCAM words to real situations.

student.intro: You know how to greet people. Now you are going to manage in everyday situations in Bulu: at the market, on the road, at home.
activities: Match each picture of a scene from daily life with the corresponding word or sentence in Bulu.
Play the role of the seller at the market: answer the requests in Bulu.
Write 5 sentences describing your morning activities from the time you wake up.
Translate these 5 sentences about daily journeys into Bulu.
Memorise 10 everyday words in Bulu with their French translation.
student.memo: The **everyday** vocabulary in **Bulu** covers food, getting around and household activities. Mastering it allows functional communication in all contexts.

lessons.title: Argue and persuade in Bulu
lessons.anelcac: Elaborate communication: argumentation, narration, formal speech
objectives: Build a simple argument in Bulu
Use the expressions of formal speech
Narrating a past event coherently
Delivering a 2-minute oral speech in Bulu

teacher.intro: Lesson: Arguing and persuading in Bulu. Module: Module VIII — Everyday life (Level 2).
steps: **Setting the context:** Read a proverb in Bulu. Ask students to explain it and defend it.
**Presentation:** Formulas of formal oral speech in Bulu: forms of address, opening, closing.
**Explanation:** Structure of an argument: thesis → arguments → examples → conclusion.
**Practice:** Debate: for or against the use of Bulu at school? Each group defends its position.
**Production:** 2-minute speech on a given theme.
teacher.freedom: Public speaking is highly valued in Cameroonian cultures. Draw on this tradition to motivate the students.
teacher.tips: Public speaking is highly valued in Cameroonian cultures. Draw on this tradition to motivate the students.

student.intro: In Bulu cultures, well-spoken words are a force. You learn to argue and persuade with eloquence.
activities: Identify in the text: thesis, arguments, examples.
Prepare 3 arguments to defend the teaching of Bulu in primary school.
Give an opening speech for a ceremony in Bulu.
Narration: tell in Bulu about a memorable event from your school life.
Memorise the opening and closing formulas of a formal speech in Bulu.
student.memo: **Argumentation** in **Bulu** follows this pattern: thesis → arguments → examples → conclusion. **Formal speech** follows precise cultural conventions. Mastery of elaborate oral expression is a high-level skill.

lessons.title: Oral literature and advanced written production
lessons.anelcac: Oral literature: proverbs, tales, riddles; long written production
objectives: Analyse the structure of a tale or a riddle in Bulu
Identify the themes and values conveyed
Writing a short tale following the conventions of the genre
Using oral literature as a teaching resource

teacher.intro: Lesson: Oral literature and advanced written production. Module: Module VIII — Everyday life (Level 2).
steps: **Setting the context:** Tell or play a short tale in Bulu.
**Presentation:** Genres of oral literature: tales, proverbs, riddles, epics.
**Analysis:** Structure of the tale: initial situation → disruption → events → resolution → moral.
**Application:** Analyse a tale provided, following this structure.
**Production:** Tale of at least 15 lines in Bulu with an explicit moral.
teacher.freedom: Oral literature is a threatened cultural treasure. Invite community storytellers if possible.
teacher.tips: Oral literature is a threatened cultural treasure. Invite community storytellers if possible.

student.intro: Bulu tales, proverbs and riddles are literary works in their own right. You will analyse them and you will create your own!
activities: Read the tale provided and identify the 5 stages of its narrative structure.
Identify 3 moral values taught by this tale.
Translate a proverb in Bulu into French and explain its figurative meaning.
Write a short tale (15 lines) in Bulu with a moral about work or respect.
Memorise: tale = fictional narrative with an educational purpose; proverb = brief formula of collective wisdom.
student.memo: The **oral literature** of **Bulu** (tales, proverbs, riddles) transmits the values of the community. The tale has a 5-stage structure. Writing it in Bulu draws on all the language skills acquired.

lessons.title: Who are the Bulu (groupement Yekombo)? Identity, language and territory
lessons.anelcac: Cultural areas, cultural identity, settlement
objectives: Name the Bulu (Yekombo group) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Bulu (Yekombo group) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where did they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Bulu (Yekombo group) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Bulu community (groupement Yekombo): who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) call themselves, and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live alongside? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Majority group, in contact with the Ngoe and the Esse, whose speech varieties it also speaks. • Bulu is spoken in Kribi, Ebolowa and as far as Gabon. • A rather mixed group; exogamy is the rule, in strict respect of kinship. • Land of the ancestors, which belongs to them; the group keeps no ties with other places of origin. • The land belongs to God; each family owns its inherited share, and there are community plots.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the majority in their group, in contact with the Ngoe and the Esse, the Bulu of Yekombo live from cocoa, food crops, fishing and basketry. Societies of families and hierarchical chiefdoms, they used to gather under the adum tree to consult the ancestors; Christianity has replaced these cults, but the cooking, the eɲəŋə dance and the bikutsi remain.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Bulu (Yekombo grouping)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
objectives: Identify traditional authorities
Explain how decisions are made
Identifying the rules of deference
lessons.competence: Describe how the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision has to be made for the whole Bulu village (groupement Yekombo). Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Bulu (Yekombo group) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “An important decision has to be made for the whole village of the Bulu (Yekombo grouping). Who decides, and how?” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Families (head of family), villages (chiefs of the 1st, 2nd and 3rd degree), notables: decisions are taken at each level, up to the sub-prefecture, by consensus after consulting the notables. • A widower and a widow may see each other freely; not so a bachelor and a married woman. • Permanent societies: mothers who specialise in burying babies, and speakers who take the floor at weddings and funerals. • The child is never right in front of his father; the wife owes respect to her husband.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Families (head of family), villages (first-, second- and third-degree chiefs), notables: decisions are taken at each level, up to the sub-prefecture, by consensus after consulting the notables. A widower and a widow may see each other freely; a single man and a married woman may not. Permanent societies: mothers who specialise in burying babies, and speakers who address the gathering at weddings and funerals.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Bulu (groupement Yekombo), then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Bulu (Yekombo grouping), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Bulu (Yekombo group), describe how they are prepared and draw out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo).” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: kpem (cassava leaves), miŋkonda (grated cassava and groundnut), saŋga (vegetables and maize), ebafon (maize and groundnut), bombo (maize cake). • Drinks: zɔŋ (aubergine infusion), palm wine. • Men: cocoa, basketry, sculpture, fishing. Women: food crops, fishing. • Ancestral crafts: baskets for carrying harvests, mortars.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Bulu (Yekombo group) eat mainly kpem, miŋkonda, saŋga, ebafon. Traditional drinks: zɔŋ, palm wine. These foods are linked to the group's activities and the produce of its environment.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)

Women: food crops, fishing. • Ancestral crafts: baskets for carrying harvests, mortars. • Beauty: the robust, tall man with a flawless face; the natural woman, with dark skin, without make-up or skin lightening.

steps.instruction: Formerly leopard skin, obom and kaba ŋkuk made of straw; today, cloth. Men: cocoa, basketry, sculpture, fishing. Women: food crops, fishing. Ancestral crafts: baskets for carrying harvests, mortars.

lessons.anelcac: Key events: birth, naming, initiation
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth

Describe the passage to adulthood
lessons.competence: Explain how the Bulu (Yekombo grouping) welcome a child, give them a name and mark their entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born into a Bulu family (groupement Yekombo). How will the child be named, and how will they become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Bulu (Yekombo group) welcome a child, give them a name and mark their entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “A child has just been born into a Bulu (Yekombo grouping) family. How will he or she be named, and how will he or she become an adult?” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The father gives each child their name; in case of separation, he may change it once. • People are addressed by their motto (eŋdán) and nicknames; the appellative is marked by a high-low tone: Ǎndəmba for Ndəmba. • The founding ancestor, Ndəmba Owutu, means “here then is Mba”. • Birth is the return of an ancestor; death, the return to the ancestors. • A boy becomes a man after twenty, when he has his house, his plantation, and offers the viper to his father.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The father gives his name to each child; in case of separation, he may change it once. People are addressed by the motto (eŋdán) and by pet names; the appellative is marked by a high-low tone: Ǎndəmba for Ndəmba. The founding ancestor, Ndəmba Owutu, means “here then is Mba”.

lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Bulu (groupement Yekombo). First you need to understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bulu (Yekombo group), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “A development project wants to help the Bulu (Yekombo grouping). First, we need to understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Men: cocoa, basketry, sculpture, fishing. Women: food crops, fishing. • Ancestral crafts: baskets for carrying the harvests, mortars.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: cocoa, basketry, sculpture, fishing. Women: food crops, fishing. Ancestral crafts: baskets for carrying harvests, mortars.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Make a two-column table (men / women) of the activities of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo), then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Find out how the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) make a living from their work.

activities.title: I classify
activities.instruction: Classify the activities in a men / women table.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain how one obtains land to cultivate.

activities.title: I calculate
activities.instruction: Imagine the calendar of a working year (seasons, harvests, festivals).

activities.title: I propose
activities.instruction: Suggest a project idea that promotes a local skill.

student.memo: Men: cocoa, basketry, sculpture, fishing. Women: food crops, fishing. Ancestral crafts: baskets for carrying harvests, mortars.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Bulu (groupement Yekombo)
lessons.anelcac: Community practices: symbolism, rites, taboos
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
Identify sacred places
Explain the role of taboos
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bulu (Yekombo grouping), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Bulu (groupement Yekombo). Which places and rules must they absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bulu (Yekombo group), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “A visitor arrives among the Bulu (Yekombo grouping). What places and rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Ancestral cults are no longer practised, replaced by Christianity. • The adum, a tree standing opposite the chiefdom, is the place where contact was made with the ancestors. • Birth is the return of an ancestor; death, the return to the ancestors. • Taboos: incest, the parents' intimate life, palavers under the adum. • Prohibitions: a boy does not eat viper without his father's consent, nor certain birds (ŋgə'ə); a pregnant woman avoids snake meat and certain cuts; one does not speak insolently to elders.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Ancestral cults are no longer practised, having been replaced by Christianity. The adum, a tree standing in front of the chiefdom, is the place where people made contact with the ancestors.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) (3 places or rules to respect, with the reason for each).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Find out what the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I identify
activities.instruction: Identify two sacred places and what they recall.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain the usefulness of a taboo for the life of the group.

activities.title: I show respect
activities.instruction: Write the guide for the respectful visitor.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare with a taboo you know in your family.

student.memo: Ancestral cults are no longer practised, having been replaced by Christianity. The adum, a tree standing in front of the chiefdom, is the place where people made contact with the ancestors.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Bulu
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day
Introducing yourself
Counting from 1 to 10
lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Bulu (groupement Yekombo) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in sharing the kola nuts while counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Bulu (groupement Yekombo) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “You are visiting a Bulu family (groupement Yekombo). Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the kola nuts by counting.” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The language of the community is Bulu. • Greeting formulas: mbolo = Hello (neutral formula, at any time); mbambatʃe = morning greeting (one person); Mbamba mos = midday greeting (one person). • Counting from 1 to 5: Fɔk, Baj, La, nin, tan. • The founding ancestor, Ndəmba Owutu, means “here then is Mba”. • Marriage, social organisation and prohibitions bring the Bulu closer to the Fang; several ancestral practices have receded in the face of Christianity.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Bulu are the first steps towards communicating with the Bulu (groupement Yekombo). Polite expressions show the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Bulu.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Bulu are the first steps towards communicating with the Bulu (groupement Yekombo). Polite expressions show the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
